scraped.description: About 86% of Black Michiganders voted for Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate, according to preliminary data.
scraped.author: Christine Slaughter
scraped.h1: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El‑Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals , as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black .

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results . Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms , up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.

In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes , which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County .

In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3% , from 50.6% in 2020 , as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide , Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll .

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed . NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson , who won the governorship over Republican John James.

Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.

Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate .

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity . Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination . If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.

My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program , while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience . El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election . Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.

“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

scraped.h1: Energy and Water Issues Propel Democrats to Victory in Arizona
scraped.body_text:
PHOENIX—Two years after President Donald Trump won Arizona with 52 percent of the vote, Democrats are poised to win a trifecta in the state House, Senate and governor’s office, and could potentially win every statewide elected position. The battleground state’s blue wave could fundamentally alter how it responds to increasingly deadly heat and persistent drought brought on by climate change.

Central to the Democrats’ wins, party members and candidates said, was their focus on addressing the state’s growing energy demand and declining water resources, which are increasingly top issues for Arizonans.

Attorney General Kris Mayes, who has made protecting the state’s water resources and fighting rising energy costs her top two priorities, won her bid for reelection. Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill took two seats on the state’s currently all-Republican commission that regulates utilities. And, for the first time since 1966, Democrats are almost guaranteed to have a trifecta with incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs winning her reelection bid against Republican-candidate Rep. Andy Biggs. Even the party’s candidate for state mine inspector, Brian Matlock , leads in the polls, with his potential win marking the first time that seat has gone to a Democrat since 1976.

Taken together, the Democrats’ wins present an opportunity for major changes to how the state approaches climate change and energy policy , potentially paving the way for new renewable energy development and groundwater regulations. The latter has proven to be one of the state’s stickiest policy debates over the last decade, and an issue where Hobbs has attempted to make strides but been stopped from enacting reform by the Republican-controlled legislature.

“What we’ve seen is data centers have brought [energy and water] issues to the forefront,” Priya Sundareshan, Democratic leader in the state Senate, told Inside Climate News at the Arizona Democrats watch party Tuesday night. “The bipartisan response to data centers that we know voters have is around their energy use and their water use, and those are fundamentally questions that we have failed to address at the state level, and we continue to fail to address because of Republican control of the legislature.”

Arizona knows extreme weather well, she said, from record-hot summers to flooding that left communities evacuated over the last week to dwindling water supplies .

“All of that is directly tied to the changing climate, and that’s something where we can tie that picture together and be able to show voters that we can see the big picture,” Sundareshan said. “We can work toward a future that makes sure that we can all live here.”

In an interview with Inside Climate News, Mayes, the attorney general, said focusing her office and campaign on energy and water issues “were pivotal” to her victory. During her first four years, Mayes sued Fondomonte Arizona, a subsidiary of a Saudi Arabian company, which was pumping an unlimited amount of water from a groundwater basin on state trust land to irrigate alfalfa that was eventually fed to cattle in Saudi Arabia. She also challenged the Arizona Corporation Commission—of which she was once an elected member—over its decisions to roll back renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. And she has called for a statewide moratorium on new data center development until a plan for them can be developed.

“I did 70 town halls all over Arizona, many of them about water and data centers,” she said. “I think that resonated with Arizonans. People are worried about our water supplies, and they didn’t think that they had politicians working hard enough on those issues, and they saw in me somebody that was willing to stick my neck out against powerful entities and I will continue to do that.”

Many of the state’s races are far from a done deal, with only a fraction of the votes counted so far. But Democrats hold overwhelming leads for many seats that put them out of reach for Republicans. The final count for the state Senate and House remain undecided, though it is clear Democrats will have a majority in both.

Democrats flipped Scottsdale’s Congressional District 1 in one of the country’s most contested races, with Dr. Amish Shah winning the seat he failed to take in 2024. They also beat incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani in southern Arizona’s Congressional District 6, with Democrat JoAnna Mendoza flipping the seat.

But it’s too early to call some of the state’s other races for the U.S. House of Representatives. Democrats are maintaining close races in three other Republican-held districts. Only one Arizona Republican, Paul Gosar, has won his reelection for his House seat so far.

Polling has consistently shown energy and water issues were top of mind for voters. The Center for the Future of Arizona found 69 percent of voters don’t have confidence that the state will have enough water in the long-term, and that water was the top issue for its voters. Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. More than 60 percent said their summer power bills are difficult to afford.

“The people of Arizona deserve leaders who are looking out for us and ensuring that we can afford to fill our gas tank and keep our lights on, and that’s why they re-elected Governor Hobbs,” said Climate Power’s Arizona State Director Diali Avila in a statement. “Andy Biggs and his fellow Republicans rubber-stamped Trump’s agenda at every turn, and now they’re paying the price. Arizonans need relief from skyrocketing costs, and Governor Hobbs will work to bring down costs for Arizonans—not enrich oil and gas billionaires.”

When Trump was elected both in 2016 and 2024, promising to make the federal government hostile to climate action, many climate advocates insisted that state and local governments would take up the mantle of pushing for clean energy. That’s the thesis of the “ America Is All In ” coalition, which brings together cities and states that have vowed to uphold America’s “climate commitments … [i]n the absence of federal leadership.” The unspoken caveat in these claims is that the states leading the way on climate policy are concentrated in a few liberal parts of the country, like New England and the West Coast.

The Democratic Party’s historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could change that. Democrats have secured control of both state legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion — also known as a “trifecta” — in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, three states that have spent years or decades under Republican or divided control. The three states have also lagged on support for clean energy. Democrats also restored trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan, and Nevada this week, but those are states where they last had unified control earlier this decade.

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy. He said that the six states where Democrats have secured trifectas would be one of the world’s largest emitters if they made up their own country, rivaling Canada and Saudi Arabia. “This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.”

Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and Arizona.

Compared to its neighbors in the Upper Midwest, Wisconsin has been far less ambitious when it comes to ditching fossil fuels in its power sector. While Michigan and Minnesota have both passed laws that mandate that the states get all their power from clean sources by 2040, Wisconsin set a measly 10 percent renewable electricity standard more than two decades ago. It blew past that goal but never set a new target. Unlike most other states, it doesn’t even require utilities to plan for what kinds of power plants they want to build. The state gets a larger share of its electricity from coal than its immediate neighbors.

Renewable energy advocates in the Badger State believe they can make some short-term gains with Democrats’ first trifecta since 2010. Erik Kanter, the policy director for the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said he believes that the new legislature can agree on the “low-hanging fruit” of making utilities plan for the future, which he said will nudge more of them to build renewables rather than extending the lifespans of gas and coal plants. The Wisconsin legislature failed this year to pass a law that would require data centers to source their power from clean sources, and Kanter expects such a measure to pass once Democrats take control. The legislature will also likely renew programs like Knowles-Nelson, a longstanding fund for parks and ecosystem preservation, which once enjoyed bipartisan approval but has lost support from Republicans in recent years.

Weiskopf, of Climate Cabinet, believes that even more ambitious moves are in the offing. He expects Wisconsin’s new class of legislators to pursue a 100 percent clean electricity standard, filling what he calls a “Wisconsin-sized hole” in the Upper Midwest. Not only would that help to phase out coal in the state, it would also make it easier for neighboring states to meet their climate goals, since the whole region shares the same interconnected power grid.

The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die. Even though the party managed to flip the lower house of the legislature a few years ago, Republican leaders in the upper chamber often refused to bring climate bills to a vote . The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.

“You don’t want to let yourself fully imagine what it can be, because you’ve been let down in the past,” said Lindsey Williams, a state senator who represents a swath of the Pittsburgh metro area. “Now we’re in that moment of, wow, there’s so many things that we can accomplish.”

Every year since 2019, Williams has introduced a bill that would establish mandatory energy and water efficiency standards for appliances like ovens and showerheads, a measure she said could save consumers millions of dollars a year. The legislation has never moved forward — but she thinks it will in next year’s session.

She hopes Democrats will use their first trifecta since 1993 to advance a full-scope climate agenda. In addition to passing laws that would allow community solar and warehouse rooftop solar , Democratic lawmakers also want to pass a funding package for struggling mass transit systems like Philadelphia’s. The $1.5 billion infusion would help prevent the transit “death spiral” for those systems and would reduce reliance on gasoline-powered cars.

The state’s reelected centrist governor, Josh Shapiro, appears to be on board with at least some of these proposals. Although he withdrew the state from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative , a Northeast-wide carbon pricing system , he has promised to create a similar cap-and-trade system for Pennsylvania itself if he can get legislative support. He has also named funding for mass transit as a leading item on his agenda for the new legislative session next year. But Democrats will have to be careful: While they will now control both chambers, they’ll have slim majorities in each, and may have just a narrow two-year window to pass climate policy before one flips back.

“We need to be brave and lead,” said Williams. “Yes, what are the low-hanging fruits, but what are the big ambitious things that we can get done this session?”

The last time Democrats had a trifecta in the Grand Canyon State was in 1966, decades before the general public was even aware of global warming. The state has ample sunshine and wind, so its renewable energy industry has grown quickly over recent years , and its grid is cleaner than in regions like the Midwest. Furthermore, the many new-built suburbs of the Phoenix metroplex tend to be heated with electricity rather than natural gas . Yet Republicans in the state legislature have all but banned climate and environmental policy, prohibiting the state government from regulating greenhouse gas emissions or energy usage, and numerous climate and water bills have failed in recent years.

Lauren Kuby, a longtime Democratic legislator who represents the Phoenix suburb of Tempe, says she and her colleagues have a long wish list that spans several issues. Their first order of business is to reform the Arizona Corporation Commission , the state’s utility regulator, which Kuby says has been slow to embrace new technologies like solar and wind even as developers seek to build more of them. Legislators want to pass a law that would direct the commission to make utilities invest in solar, batteries, and “virtual power plants,” or networks of homes and businesses that coordinate their energy usage. As part of the reform, they might even change the commission’s name, taking out the “corporation” and replacing it with “public utilities.” The two Democrats who appear set to win seats on the commission will make these reforms easier to push through.

The legislature could also break long-standing logjams on the crucial issue of water — a scarce resource in a desert state where climate change is worsening droughts. Kuby and other senators have been trying for years to pass a bill that would regulate groundwater pumping in the state’s rural areas. These areas are home to massive dairies and alfalfa farms like Riverview and the Saudi-backed Fondomonte , which have been blamed for sinking land and dried-up residential wells. The bill has failed in several legislative sessions , but Kuby believes that some form of regulation can pass in the coming year, bringing an end to the water free-for-all in the desert areas outside Phoenix.

“That has been languishing and has not been heard in the legislature, even though we have agreement from a lot of Republicans on water and environmental protection,” said Kuby. Of the trifecta, she said, “It’s a game-changer.”
